analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: לְנַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם qualifies דִּמְכֶם, “your blood.” God requires an accounting for shed blood because it represents the lives taken. The closing אֶדְרֹשׁ אֶת נֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם makes the object of that accounting explicit as human life.
analysis.morphology: The preposition לְ introduces the common-gender noun in the plural construct. The second-person masculine plural suffix כֶם identifies the lives as those of the addressees.
analysis.sense: the life that is in the blood

analysis.evidence: The direct object אֶת־דִּמְכֶם means “your blood.” The repeated מִיַּד (“from the hand of”) identifies those whom God will hold accountable for that blood, whether animal or human.
analysis.gloss: I will demand an accounting for
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, first person common singular. The אֶ־ marks first person singular. The verb has no pronominal suffix.

analysis.evidence: In מִיַּד כָּל חַיָּה, “from the hand of every animal,” כָּל gives the indefinite singular חַיָּה distributive force. Each animal is individually accountable for human bloodshed.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state before חַיָּה.

analysis.evidence: מִיַּד כָּל חַיָּה means “from the hand of every animal.” The parallel וּמִיַּד הָאָדָם, “and from the hand of the human,” identifies animals and humans as those from whom God will demand an accounting for human blood.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the absolute state, governed by the construct כָּל.

analysis.evidence: The suffix refers back to דִּמְכֶם, “your blood,” the object of the preceding אֶדְרֹשׁ. The phrase מִיַּד כָּל חַיָּה identifies every animal as accountable for that blood.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, first person common singular, with a third person masculine singular direct-object suffix.
